b1_sentences: On July 15, 2026, England and Argentina met in Atlanta.
Their famous rivalry produced a finish few expected after a quiet first half.
Neither team had a shot on target before the break.
The challenges were strong and the tension was high, but no goal came.
The game changed in the 55th minute.
Rogers sent a cross into the area, and Gordon scored to put England ahead.
England could finally dream of their first World Cup final since 1966.
With five minutes left, England strengthened their defense.
They seemed ready to protect their lead and enter the final.
But Messi found Enzo Fernández in the 85th minute.
Enzo hit a powerful shot to make the score 1–1.
Then stoppage time began.
Messi crossed from the right, and substitute Lautaro Martínez scored with a strong header.
In only seven minutes, England’s joy had turned into pain.
England 1–2 Argentina
At 39, the Argentina captain made two assists.
He did not take either of the final shots.
Instead, Messi created the chances for Enzo and Lautaro to score the decisive goals.
He showed again that a player can control and finish a game without scoring.
England took off players including Rice and made its defense stronger.
The team wanted to protect its narrow lead.
Argentina made the opposite choice.
In the 81st minute, defender Tagliafico went off and striker Lautaro Martínez came on.
Lautaro later scored the winning goal.
Each team’s substitutions showed its plan.
In the end, those choices helped decide the result.
“England tried to close the door to the final.
Messi slipped two keys through the gap.”
Argentina will now face Spain, with a second straight title possible.
England must live with the painful memory of those final five minutes.
a2_sentences: Argentina beat England 2–1 in Atlanta on July 15, 2026.
England led until the 85th minute.
Then Messi created two goals in seven minutes.
Argentina reached the World Cup final against Spain.
The first half was quiet but tense.
Neither team had a shot on target.
England took the lead in the 55th minute.
Rogers crossed the ball, and Gordon scored.
England started to dream of the final.
It was England’s first possible final since 1966.
But Argentina fought back in the 85th minute.
Messi passed to Enzo Fernández.
Enzo hit a powerful shot and made the score 1–1.
Messi created another chance during stoppage time.
He crossed from the right.
Lautaro Martínez headed the ball into the goal.
Messi, 39, made both assists.
He did not score, but he controlled the ending.
England tried to protect its lead.
The team took off players including Rice.
England also made its defense stronger.
Argentina chose a different plan.
In the 81st minute, Argentina took off defender Tagliafico.
Striker Lautaro Martínez came onto the field.
Lautaro then scored the winning goal.
The teams’ different choices changed the match.
England tried to protect its lead, but Messi opened the way to Argentina’s 2–1 win.

b1_sentences: At midnight, social media may soon start telling teenagers in the UK, “Goodnight.”
On July 15, the British government announced a planned digital switch-off period for 16- and 17-year-olds.
It would run from midnight until 6 a.m.
During these hours, covered apps would be unavailable under the standard settings.
Notifications would pause, and autoplay would be switched off.
Autoplay is the feature that starts each new video automatically.
Personalized feeds would also stop during this period.
These feeds suggest content and encourage users to continue scrolling.
The measures are expected to begin in spring 2027.
However, this would not be a complete ban.
Teenagers aged 16 and 17 could change the settings and opt out.
This raises an obvious question.
Would everyone simply turn the restrictions off?
Perhaps some would.
But the plan focuses on changing the standard experience rather than giving strict orders.
To open an app overnight, users would need to stop and actively change the setting.
The government hopes this small extra step will slow the urge to watch “just one more” video.
A trial involving 309 families tested three different approaches.
Nighttime restrictions ran from 9 p.m. until 7 a.m.
Families found this approach the easiest to manage.
They also reported the most regular improvements in sleep.
However, some teenagers moved their screen time to just before or after the restricted hours.
This shows that nighttime limits cannot make the wider problem disappear by themselves.
Ofcom carried out a separate experiment with children.
One setting stopped apps from recommending harmful content.
When this was the standard setting, about seven in ten children kept it.
When no choice was already selected, only about half chose the safer setting.
The setting was not required.
Still, the results suggest that standard settings can strongly influence people’s choices.
The UK wants to switch off not the smartphone’s light, but the endless scrolling that keeps teenagers awake.
This midnight limit stands between a strict ban and doing nothing.
Its success will depend on how many teenagers leave it unchanged and simply go to sleep.
a2_sentences: The UK plans a nighttime break from social media.
The British government announced the plan on July 15.
It covers teenagers aged 16 and 17.
The plan should start in spring 2027.
Apps under the plan will be unavailable by default overnight.
The break will last from midnight to 6 a.m.
Notifications will pause during these hours.
Autoplay will also stop.
Autoplay starts a new video after one ends.
Personal recommendation feeds will also stop.
These feeds can keep users scrolling for hours.
Teenagers can turn the settings off.
So this is not a full ban.
The plan adds one extra step before late-night use.
A trial with 309 families tested three different plans.
Families found the nighttime plan easiest to manage.
It stopped screen use from 9 p.m. to 7 a.m.
Families reported better sleep most consistently with this plan.
However, some teenagers moved their screen time.
They used screens just before or after the blocked hours.
So a nighttime break may not fix the wider problem.
Ofcom ran a separate test with children.
One setting stopped apps from suggesting harmful content.
For some children, the test turned on this setting first.
About seven in ten of these children kept it.
For another group, the test chose no setting first.
Around half of this group chose the same setting.
The setting was optional for everyone.
Still, the results suggest defaults can guide people’s choices.
The UK plan uses the same idea.
Teenagers must turn off the nighttime setting first.
This small step may stop some late-night scrolling.
The UK wants a nighttime pause to help more teenagers put down their phones and sleep.

b1_sentences: Imagine a giant tollbooth suddenly appearing in the Strait of Hormuz.
On July 13, 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump announced a new plan.
He wanted to collect 20 percent of the value of all cargo passing through the strait.
He said the money would pay for keeping this important waterway safe.
But the plan was withdrawn just one day later.
Gulf nations would instead seek trade and investment deals with the United States.
It was unclear how much money was involved or which countries would take part.
The message changed overnight from “Pay 20 percent to pass” to “Invest in the United States instead.”
Within 24 hours, the plan had changed completely.
But did the oil markets feel calmer?
Only partly.
Brent crude oil had risen about 10 percent the day before.
Tensions between the United States and Iran were growing.
The proposed 20 percent charge also shocked the market.
After the plan was canceled, oil fell from a daily high above $87 a barrel.
However, Brent closed at $84.73 on July 14.
That was still about 2 percent higher and its highest level in a month.
The reason was simple.
The fee was gone, but other dangers remained.
A blockade against ships linked to Iran was still in place.
Military attacks were also continuing.
The market was not only worried about the cost of passing through the strait.
The bigger question was whether ships could pass through safely.
A fully loaded Very Large Crude Carrier could have faced a fee of about $30 million.
That is roughly 4.9 billion yen.
The shipping industry had received no warning before the announcement.
It was therefore not surprising that the plan caused shock and serious doubts.
On July 13, the International Maritime Organization repeated an important rule.
Under international law, ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz should not pay tolls or transit fees.
The proposal did more than make markets nervous.
It also went directly against the basic principle of freedom of navigation.
“The tollbooth sign is gone, but the smell of gunpowder still hangs over the strait.”
Changing the policy may calm the headlines.
But markets will not truly relax until ships can pass through the Strait of Hormuz without fear.

The fee covered all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
It was 20 percent of the cargo’s value.
Trump dropped the plan one day later.
Gulf nations would seek trade and investment deals with the United States instead.
The countries and money amounts remained unclear.
Oil prices fell, but the market stayed worried.
The proposed fee could cost one large oil tanker $30 million.
That equals about 4.9 billion yen.
The shipping industry received no warning before the announcement.
The plan caused shock and doubt across the industry.
The plan also raised questions about international law.
The International Maritime Organization repeated an important rule on July 13.
Ships should not pay fees to pass through the strait.
This rule supports free travel at sea.
Brent crude oil rose about 10 percent before Trump dropped the plan.
U.S.-Iran tensions and the proposed fee pushed prices higher.
Brent later fell from a daily high above $87 per barrel.
Still, Brent ended July 14 at $84.73.
This was about 2 percent higher.
It was also the highest price in one month.
Other dangers remained in the area.
A blockade still targeted ships linked to Iran.
Military attacks also continued.
The market cared about more than the fee.
Ships also needed safe travel through the strait.
The 20 percent fee disappeared, but serious risks remained in the Strait of Hormuz.
